topics.name: Acts of the Apostles
topics.kicker: New Testament history of the early Church · Pentecost and Paul’s journeys
topics.dates: Usually dated to the late 1st century CE
topics.briefing: In the Acts of the Apostles, the fifth book of the New Testament, a rushing wind fills a room in Jerusalem and tongues of fire rest on Jesus’s followers, who begin speaking in languages they never learned. That scene, called Pentecost, launches the book’s story of the early Church spreading from Jerusalem toward Rome. Its second half follows Paul through riots, prison, and a shipwreck on Malta.
topics.answerHtml: Acts of the Apostles (or Book of Acts; prompt on Luke-Acts)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Parts of this book switch from telling what “they” did to what “we” did, suggesting to many readers that its author traveled with its main missionary. Like an earlier book by the same author, this book is addressed to a man named Theophilus [“thee-OFF-ih-lus”].
tossups.r: Tradition says both books were written by Luke. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: In this book, a young man named Eutychus [“YOO-tih-kus”] falls asleep during a long sermon and drops from a third-story window, but the preacher brings him back to life. Later in this book, that preacher survives a shipwreck on Malta and shakes off a snake that bites his hand.
tossups.r: That preacher, Paul, ends this book under house arrest in Rome. For 10 points, name this New Testament book that comes right after the Gospels.

tossups.p: In this book, the church in Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul on a mission to the island of Cyprus. This book also says that the followers of Jesus were first called “Christians” in Antioch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this book of the Bible that describes the Holy Spirit coming down at Pentecost.

tossups.p: The word “simony” [“SY-muh-nee”], for buying or selling church offices, comes from a magician in this book who offers the apostles money for the power to give people the Holy Spirit. Earlier in this book, a couple named Ananias and Sapphira die suddenly after lying to Peter about money from selling their land.
tossups.r: This book begins with Jesus rising into heaven. For 10 points, name this New Testament book about the early Church.

tossups.p: In this book, a speaker in Athens points to an altar inscribed “To an unknown god” in a speech at the Areopagus [“air-ee-OP-uh-gus”], or Mars Hill. In that speech, he says that in God “we live and move and have our being.”
tossups.r: That speaker, Paul, makes several missionary journeys in this book. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: In this book, a seller of purple cloth named Lydia, often called the first recorded convert in Europe, is baptized at Philippi. Later in Philippi, an earthquake shakes open the doors of a prison where two missionaries have been singing hymns at midnight, and their jailer is baptized.
tossups.r: Those missionaries were Paul and Silas. For 10 points, name this New Testament book that ends with Paul in Rome.

tossups.p: In this book, the evangelist Philip meets a court official of the queen of Ethiopia who is reading the prophet Isaiah while riding in his chariot. Philip explains the passage to him, and the official is baptized in water beside the road.
tossups.r: This book also describes Saul’s conversion on the road to Damascus. For 10 points, name this book that follows the Gospel of John.

tossups.p: In this book, Peter has a vision of a great sheet full of animals that the Law of Moses called unclean, and a voice tells him not to call anything unclean that God has made clean. He then has a Roman centurion named Cornelius [“kor-NEEL-yus”] and his household baptized.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Testament book whose second chapter describes the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

tossups.p: In the fifteenth chapter of this book, a council in Jerusalem decides, on the advice of James, that non-Jewish believers do not have to follow the whole Law of Moses, after Peter, Barnabas, and Paul describe their work among the Gentiles.
tossups.r: This book also tells of Stephen, the first Christian martyr. For 10 points, name this book written by the author of the Gospel of Luke.

tossups.p: In this book, the respected teacher Gamaliel [“guh-MAY-lee-ul”] advises the council called the Sanhedrin [“san-HEE-drin”] to leave the apostles alone, saying that if their movement comes from God, no one will be able to stop it. Paul later says that he studied under Gamaliel.
tossups.r: This book also describes how the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost. For 10 points, name this book that tells the history of the early Church.

tossups.p: Near the start of this book, Peter stands up among about 120 believers, and they cast lots to choose Matthias [“muh-THY-us”] over Joseph Barsabbas [“bar-SAB-us”] to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve.
tossups.r: This book later follows Paul’s missionary journeys. For 10 points, name this New Testament book written by the author of Luke’s Gospel.

tossups.p: In this book, an angel leads Peter out of prison, and when he knocks at the gate of a house where believers are praying, a servant girl named Rhoda is so overjoyed that she runs inside to tell them without opening the gate.
tossups.r: This book also describes Pentecost and the conversion of Saul. For 10 points, name this New Testament book.

tossups.p: In this book, a silversmith named Demetrius, who made small silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, stirs up a riot in Ephesus, and the crowd shouts “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for about two hours.
tossups.r: The missionary whose preaching angered Demetrius was Paul. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: After a man who had never walked is healed at Lystra [“LISS-truh”] in this book, the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and his companion as Hermes, and the two missionaries tear their clothes to stop the people from offering sacrifices to them.
tossups.r: That companion was Paul, who had been blinded by a light on the road to Damascus. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, one of seven men chosen to hand out food to widows gives a long speech retelling Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon. The witnesses at that man’s death laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
tossups.r: That man, Stephen, became the first Christian martyr when a crowd stoned him. For 10 points, name this New Testament book.

clues.t: Fifth book of the New Testament, right after the four Gospels; it tells the history of the early Church
Written by the author of the Gospel of Luke, traditionally Luke the physician
Chapter 2: at Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes as tongues of fire, and the apostles speak in other languages
Follows Paul’s missionary journeys and ends with him under house arrest in Rome
Saul is blinded by a light on the road to Damascus and becomes a follower of Jesus
Like Luke’s Gospel, it is addressed to a man named Theophilus
Begins with Jesus’s ascension into heaven, forty days after his resurrection
Stephen, one of seven chosen helpers, becomes the first Christian martyr when a crowd stones him
Matthias is chosen by casting lots to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve
Believers are first called “Christians” at Antioch, whose church sends Barnabas and Saul on a mission to Cyprus
The Council of Jerusalem (chapter 15) rules that non-Jewish believers need not follow the whole Law of Moses
Peter’s vision of a sheet of unclean animals; then the Roman centurion Cornelius is baptized
Ananias and Sapphira die suddenly after lying to Peter about money from a land sale
Its first half centers on Peter, and its second half centers on Paul
The “we” passages, told in the first person plural, suggest that the author traveled with Paul
Simon Magus tries to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit, which gives us the word “simony”
Philip baptizes an Ethiopian court official who was reading Isaiah in his chariot
Paul preaches at the Areopagus (Mars Hill) in Athens about an altar “to an unknown god”
In Philippi, Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, is baptized; an earthquake opens the prison of Paul and Silas, and their jailer is baptized
Eutychus falls asleep during Paul’s long sermon, drops from a third-story window, and is brought back to life
Paul is shipwrecked on Malta and shakes off a viper without harm
An angel frees Peter from prison; the servant girl Rhoda is so excited she forgets to open the gate
Gamaliel, Paul’s teacher, tells the Sanhedrin that if the apostles’ movement is from God, it cannot be stopped
Demetrius the silversmith starts a riot in Ephesus: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
At Lystra, crowds hail Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes
Stephen’s long speech retells Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon; witnesses laid their cloaks at Saul’s feet

trap.title: The book, not its heroes
trap.body: Most clues follow Peter or Paul, so early buzzers name a person instead of the book. Others hear “by the author of Luke” or “addressed to Theophilus” and answer the Gospel of Luke, the first half of the same two-part work. Paul’s own letters, such as Romans and Galatians, are separate books.
trap.fix: If the question says “this book,” answer “Acts” (or “Acts of the Apostles”). Theophilus plus Jesus’s birth or parables means the Gospel of Luke; Theophilus plus Pentecost, Stephen, or Paul’s journeys means Acts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Acts of the Apostles (or Book of Acts; prompt on Luke-Acts)

topics.name: Judaism
topics.kicker: Monotheistic faith of the Torah · Synagogues, Sabbath, and Talmud
topics.briefing: Judaism is the oldest of the three major Abrahamic religions, which all worship one God. Jews trace their faith to God’s covenant with Abraham and to the Torah, which tradition says Moses received on Mount Sinai. Every week, many Jewish families welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening with candles, blessings over wine and braided challah bread, and a day of rest that lasts until Saturday night.
topics.answerHtml: Judaism (accept Jews or Jewish faith; do not accept “Hebrew” or “Torah”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a Talmud story, a man promised to join this religion if the sage Hillel could teach him its entire law while he stood on one foot. Hillel replied, “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor,” and said that everything else was commentary.
tossups.r: Its followers celebrate Passover and Hanukkah. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers worship in synagogues.

tossups.p: The medieval philosopher Maimonides [“my-MON-ih-deez”] listed this religion’s core beliefs as Thirteen Principles of Faith and wrote the _Guide for the Perplexed_, which tries to bring its teachings into harmony with the philosophy of Aristotle. He also wrote a law code called the _Mishneh Torah_.
tossups.r: This religion’s holiest day is Yom Kippur. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Torah.

tossups.p: Around 200 CE, Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi [“hah-NAH-see”] gathered this religion’s oral laws into the Mishnah [“MISH-nuh”], which is divided into six orders. Later discussions of the Mishnah by rabbis, called the Gemara [“guh-MAR-uh”], were joined to it to form the Talmud.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers celebrate Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: A small case called a mezuzah [“meh-ZOO-zuh”], fixed to the doorposts of many homes in this religion, holds a tiny parchment scroll with the Shema [“shuh-MAH”], a prayer that begins “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”
tossups.r: Its houses of worship are called synagogues. For 10 points, name this religion whose holidays include Passover and Rosh Hashanah.

tossups.p: In the 1700s, Israel ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov [“BAHL shem TOHV”], founded the Hasidic [“huh-SID-ik”] movement in this religion in Eastern Europe, teaching that joyful prayer, song, and sincere devotion matter as much as scholarship.
tossups.r: Its major branches include Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform. For 10 points, name this religion of the Torah.

tossups.p: This religion’s Bible is called the Tanakh [“tah-NAHK”], a name formed from the Hebrew first letters of its three parts: the Law, the Prophets (Nevi’im), and the Writings (Ketuvim). Its books are traditionally counted as 24.
tossups.r: The first part, the Torah, is traditionally said to have been given to Moses on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Under this religion’s dietary laws, called kashrut [“kahsh-ROOT”], land animals must both chew their cud and have split hooves, and seafood must have both fins and scales, so pork and shellfish are forbidden, and so are many birds of prey.
tossups.r: Followers who keep these laws also separate meat from dairy, and food that follows them is called kosher. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The _Zohar_, the central book of this religion’s mystical tradition, Kabbalah [“kuh-BAH-luh”], was long credited to the second-century rabbi Simeon bar Yochai [“bar YOH-khye”], but most scholars think Moses de León [“day lay-OHN”] wrote it in 13th-century Spain.
tossups.r: This religion’s teachers are called rabbis. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy texts include the Torah and Talmud.

tossups.p: During the Second Temple period, this religion’s groups included the Sadducees [“SAD-joo-seez”], who accepted only the written law, and the Pharisees [“FAIR-ih-seez”], whose belief in an oral law shaped the rabbis who came after them. A third group, the Essenes, may have written the Dead Sea Scrolls.
tossups.r: Its scripture is the Hebrew Bible. For 10 points, name this religion that grew from the faith of the ancient Israelites.

tossups.p: Karaite [“KAIR-uh-ite”] followers of this religion reject the Talmud and follow only the written Bible. Its Ashkenazi [“ahsh-kuh-NAH-zee”] communities come from Central and Eastern Europe, while its Sephardi [“seh-FAR-dee”] communities trace their roots to Spain and Portugal.
tossups.r: Its followers rest on a weekly day called Shabbat and worship in synagogues. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Public prayer in this religion traditionally requires a minyan [“MIN-yun”], a quorum of ten. When its sacred scroll is read aloud, the reader follows the text with a pointer called a yad [“YAHD”], meaning “hand,” so that the parchment is not touched.
tossups.r: That scroll holds the Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, a leader of the Haskalah [“hahs-kah-LAH”], or Enlightenment, within this religion, translated the Torah into German in the 1780s. In the early 1800s, its Reform movement began in Germany, holding some services in German instead of Hebrew.
tossups.r: Its other branches include Orthodox and Conservative. For 10 points, name this religion that celebrates Passover and Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: Observant followers of this religion avoid 39 categories of work on their weekly day of rest, and some neighborhoods are surrounded by an eruv [“AIR-uv”], a boundary line that lets people carry things outdoors on that day.
tossups.r: That day of rest, the Sabbath, or Shabbat, lasts from Friday sunset to Saturday night. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The scholar Rashi [“RAH-shee”], who lived in Troyes [“TRWAH”], France, in the 1000s, wrote line-by-line commentaries on this religion’s Bible and Talmud. Those commentaries are still printed beside the texts in a special typeface named for him.
tossups.r: Its followers celebrate the Sabbath each week and holidays such as Purim and Passover. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Joseph Karo’s 16th-century law code, the _Shulchan Aruch_ [“SHOOL-khahn AH-rookh”], or “Set Table,” became a standard guide to this religion’s practice. At age 13, boys in this religion become a bar mitzvah [“bar MITS-vuh”], or “son of the commandment.”
tossups.r: Many girls celebrate a bat mitzvah at 12 or 13. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Torah.

clues.t: The oldest of the three major Abrahamic faiths; followers believe God made a covenant with Abraham
Holiest text: the Torah, the five books of Moses, from Genesis to Deuteronomy
Followers worship in synagogues and learn from teachers called rabbis
Holidays include Passover, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hanukkah, and Purim
The Sabbath (Shabbat) lasts from Friday sunset to Saturday night
Symbols include the six-pointed Star of David and the menorah
Its Bible, the Tanakh (24 books), has three parts: Torah (Law), Nevi’im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings)
The Talmud combines the Mishnah (oral law, written down around 200 CE) and the Gemara (later rabbis’ discussions)
The Shema prayer, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one,” is written inside each mezuzah
Kosher dietary laws (kashrut) forbid pork and shellfish and keep meat and dairy apart
At 13, a boy becomes a bar mitzvah (“son of the commandment”); many girls have a bat mitzvah at 12 or 13
Main branches: Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform
Followers believe God gave the Torah to Moses on Mount Sinai; tradition counts 613 commandments (mitzvot) in it
Ashkenazi communities come from Central and Eastern Europe (Yiddish); Sephardi communities from Spain and Portugal (Ladino)
Maimonides wrote the Thirteen Principles of Faith, the _Mishneh Torah_, and the _Guide for the Perplexed_
Asked to teach the whole law while the asker stood on one foot, Hillel said, “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor”; the rest is commentary
Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi compiled the Mishnah, in six orders, around 200 CE
The Baal Shem Tov founded Hasidism in 1700s Eastern Europe, stressing joyful prayer and devotion
Kabbalah, its mystical tradition, centers on the _Zohar_, probably written by Moses de León in 13th-century Spain
Second Temple groups: Sadducees (written law only), Pharisees (oral law), and Essenes (possibly the Dead Sea Scrolls)
Karaites reject the Talmud and follow only the written Bible
Rashi of Troyes, France, wrote famous commentaries on the Bible and Talmud, printed in “Rashi script”
Joseph Karo’s 16th-century law code, the _Shulchan Aruch_ (“Set Table”)
Moses Mendelssohn led the Haskalah (Enlightenment); the Reform movement began in Germany in the early 1800s
Observant followers avoid 39 categories of work on the Sabbath; an eruv boundary lets people carry things outdoors
Public prayer needs a minyan (a quorum of ten); the Torah scroll is read with a pointer called a yad (“hand”)

trap.title: Religion, book, or language?
trap.body: Several near-miss answers circle this one: the Torah is its holiest text, Hebrew is its sacred language, and Israel is both the ancient people’s name and a modern country. None of those is the religion itself. Christianity and Islam also honor Abraham and Moses, so a patriarch or prophet clue alone is not enough.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this religion” or “this faith,” say Judaism (“Jews” or “Jewish” also works). Say Torah only for “this text,” Hebrew only for “this language,” and Talmud only for “this collection” of rabbinic writings. Rabbis, synagogues, kosher laws, and the Shema point to Judaism.
trap.line: Real answer line: Judaism (accept Jews or Jewish faith; do not accept “Hebrew” or “Torah”)

topics.name: Shinto
topics.kicker: Native religion of Japan · Kami spirits, shrines, and torii gates
topics.dates: Ancient · Myths first written down in 712 CE
topics.briefing: Walk through an orange-red torii gate in Japan and you enter a Shinto shrine, a place where people honor kami: spirits believed to dwell in mountains, waterfalls, and ancient trees, in ancestors, and even in great scholars. Shinto has no founder and no single holy book, but its myths, written down in the _Kojiki_ in 712 CE, tell how the sun goddess Amaterasu became the ancestor of Japan’s emperors.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The scholar Motoori Norinaga [“moh-toh-OH-ree noh-ree-NAH-gah”] spent decades writing a commentary on the _Kojiki_ [“KOH-jee-kee”], hoping to recover the beliefs of this religion as they were before Buddhism and Confucianism reached Japan. He belonged to the National Learning, or Kokugaku [“koh-koo-GAH-koo”], movement of the 1700s.
tossups.r: Its spirits are called kami. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose shrines are marked by torii gates.

tossups.p: Every 20 years, the main buildings of this religion’s holiest shrine, at Ise [“EE-say”], are rebuilt on a neighboring site using the same ancient methods, a ritual that was held for the 62nd time in 2013. That ritual is called the Shikinen Sengu [“shee-kee-NEN SEN-goo”].
tossups.r: That shrine honors the sun goddess Amaterasu. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In 712 CE, the court official Ō no Yasumaro [“OH noh yah-soo-MAH-roh”] wrote down myths that Hieda no Are [“hee-EH-dah noh AH-reh”] had memorized, producing the _Kojiki_, a key text of this religion. The _Nihon Shoki_ [“nee-HOHN SHOH-kee”] followed in 720.
tossups.r: Those books tell of spirits called kami, such as the sun goddess Amaterasu. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In this religion’s creation story, the divine couple Izanagi [“ee-zah-NAH-gee”] and Izanami [“ee-zah-NAH-mee”] stirred the ocean with a jeweled spear, and the drops that fell from its tip formed the first island. They went on to create the islands of Japan.
tossups.r: The sun goddess Amaterasu was born when Izanagi washed his left eye. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In one myth of this religion, the world went dark when the sun goddess shut herself in a cave, until the goddess Ame-no-Uzume [“AH-meh noh oo-ZOO-meh”] danced on an overturned tub so wildly that the other gods roared with laughter. A mirror hung outside helped draw the sun goddess back out.
tossups.r: That sun goddess, Amaterasu, is honored at the Ise Shrine. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In a myth of this religion, the storm god Susanoo [“soo-SAH-noh-oh”] tricked the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi [“yah-MAH-tah noh oh-ROH-chee”] and slew it, then found the sword Kusanagi [“koo-sah-NAH-gee”] inside one of its tails. Susanoo did this to save a young woman named Kushinada-hime [“koo-shee-NAH-dah HEE-meh”], whom he then married.
tossups.r: That sword became one of Japan’s three Imperial Regalia. For 10 points, name this religion, whose kami include Susanoo’s sister Amaterasu.

tossups.p: In this religion’s myths, the sun goddess gave her grandson Ninigi [“nee-NEE-gee”] a mirror, a sword, and a jewel when she sent him down from heaven to rule Japan. Ninigi’s great-grandson Jimmu was said to be the first emperor.
tossups.r: Those three treasures became the Imperial Regalia. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, which honors kami.

tossups.p: In 1868, Japan’s new Meiji [“MAY-jee”] government ordered this religion’s shrines to be separated from Buddhist temples and later promoted a state form of this religion. After World War II, a 1945 directive from the Allied occupation ended government support for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose priests serve spirits called kami.

tossups.p: Students often pray for success on exams at shrines of this religion devoted to Tenjin [“TEN-jin”], the spirit of the scholar Sugawara no Michizane [“soo-gah-WAH-rah noh mee-chee-ZAH-neh”], who came to be honored as a spirit of learning after his death.
tossups.r: Visitors write their wishes on small wooden plaques called ema. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose shrines are marked by torii.

tossups.p: Statues of foxes, believed to be messengers of the rice deity Inari [“ee-NAH-ree”], guard many shrines of this religion. The head shrine of Inari, Fushimi Inari [“foo-SHEE-mee ee-NAH-ree”] in Kyoto, sits at the foot of a sacred mountain.
tossups.r: Thousands of bright orange torii gates line the paths up that mountain. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: Before approaching a shrine of this religion, visitors rinse their hands and mouth with water from a stone basin, a purification rite called temizu [“teh-MEE-zoo”]. Priests also purify worshippers by waving a wooden wand covered with white paper streamers.
tossups.r: The entrance to such a shrine is marked by a gateway called a torii. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Thick ropes of rice straw called shimenawa [“shee-meh-NAH-wah”], often hung with zigzag strips of white paper, mark trees, rocks, and other places that this religion treats as sacred. Sumo wrestlers toss salt into the ring before bouts, a purification ritual with roots in this religion.
tossups.r: Many of those sacred places are believed to be home to spirits called kami. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: The shrine of Itsukushima [“ee-tsoo-koo-SHEE-mah”] on the island of Miyajima [“mee-yah-JEE-mah”] is built over the water, so that at high tide it seems to float. Its huge gate, which stands in the sea, is one of Japan’s most famous sights.
tossups.r: That gate is a torii, the symbol of this religion’s shrines. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: On the festival of Shichi-Go-San [“shee-chee-goh-SAHN”], or “Seven-Five-Three,” families take children of those ages to shrines of this religion to pray for their health. Millions of people also visit those shrines in the first days of each new year, a custom called hatsumode [“hah-tsoo-MOH-deh”].
tossups.r: Festivals called matsuri often feature portable shrines carried through the streets. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, which honors spirits called kami.

tossups.p: For centuries, many people in Japan treated this religion’s spirits as local forms of buddhas, an idea called honji suijaku [“HOHN-jee soo-ee-JAH-koo”]. Babies are often blessed at this religion’s shrines, but because it links death with impurity, most funerals in Japan follow Buddhist rites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, centered on shrines and spirits called kami.

clues.t: Native religion of Japan, with no founder and no single holy book
Honors kami: spirits or gods believed to be present in nature, places, ancestors, and great people
Its shrines are marked by torii, gateways that are often painted orange-red
The sun goddess Amaterasu is its most important kami; in myth, Japan’s emperors descend from her
Its name means “way of the gods”
Ise Grand Shrine, its holiest shrine, honors Amaterasu and is rebuilt every 20 years
Key texts: the _Kojiki_ (712) and _Nihon Shoki_ (720), Japan’s oldest books of myths and history
Creator couple Izanagi and Izanami stirred the sea with a jeweled spear to make the first island
Amaterasu hid in a cave and the world went dark until Ame-no-Uzume’s dance and a mirror drew her out
Storm god Susanoo slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi and found the sword Kusanagi in its tail
Three Imperial Regalia: a mirror, a sword (Kusanagi), and a jewel
Purification is central: visitors rinse hands and mouth (temizu) before praying, and priests wave paper-streamer wands
Mixed with Buddhism for centuries until the Meiji government separated them in 1868
Festivals (matsuri) carry portable shrines (mikoshi) through the streets
Motoori Norinaga, a National Learning (Kokugaku) scholar of the 1700s, studied the _Kojiki_ to recover pre-Buddhist beliefs
Ō no Yasumaro wrote the _Kojiki_ from myths memorized by Hieda no Are
Amaterasu’s grandson Ninigi came down to rule Japan; his great-grandson Jimmu was, in myth, the first emperor
A 1945 directive from the Allied occupation ended state support for this faith after World War II
Tenjin, the spirit of the scholar Sugawara no Michizane, is honored for learning; students pray at his shrines before exams
Inari, the kami of rice, uses foxes as messengers; Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari shrine has thousands of torii
Shimenawa (rice-straw ropes) hung with zigzag paper strips mark sacred places
Sumo wrestlers throw salt into the ring to purify it, a ritual rooted in this faith
Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima seems to float at high tide, and its torii stands in the sea
Shichi-Go-San: children aged 3, 5, and 7 visit shrines; hatsumode is the first shrine visit of the new year
Honji suijaku: the idea that kami are local forms of buddhas
Death is linked with impurity (kegare), so most funerals are Buddhist, while babies are blessed at shrines
Visitors write wishes on wooden plaques called ema

trap.title: Religion or spirits?
trap.body: Shinto clues are full of kami, the spirits it honors, and some tossups ask for the kami themselves, so answering “kami” to a question about the religion (or “Shinto” to a question about the spirits) loses the points. Buddhism is the other trap: most people in Japan take part in both, and shrines and temples often stand side by side.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun: “these spirits” or “these beings” means kami; “this religion” or “this faith” means Shinto (or Shintoism). Shrines, torii, Amaterasu, and the _Kojiki_ mean Shinto; temples, pagodas, Zen, and the Buddha mean Buddhism.

topics.name: Book of Genesis
topics.kicker: First book of the Bible · Creation, Noah, and the patriarchs
topics.briefing: The Bible’s very first words, “In the beginning,” open the Book of Genesis, which runs from the story of creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt. Along the way come some of the most famous stories ever told: Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, Noah’s ark, the Tower of Babel, and the families of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “origin.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On Christmas Eve 1968, astronauts Bill Anders, Jim Lovell, and Frank Borman took turns reading the first ten verses of this book on live television while orbiting the Moon aboard Apollo 8, the first crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon.
tossups.r: Those verses describe the first days of creation, including God saying “Let there be light.” For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: John Steinbeck took the title of a 1952 novel from a verse in this book, and characters in that novel debate the meaning of a Hebrew word from it, timshel [“TIM-shel”], which they translate as “thou mayest.”
tossups.r: That novel, _East of Eden_, retells this book’s story of Cain and Abel. For 10 points, name this first book of the Torah.

tossups.p: This book says that a river flowing out of a garden split into four branches: the Pishon [“PEE-shon”], the Gihon [“GEE-hon”], the Tigris, and the Euphrates [“yoo-FRAY-teez”]. Cherubim and a flaming sword later guarded the way to that garden’s tree of life.
tossups.r: That garden was Eden, home of Adam and Eve. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: Scholars who follow the documentary hypothesis say this book weaves together older sources, such as the ones they call J and P, which would explain why it seems to tell one story twice, in its first and second chapters.
tossups.r: In those chapters, God creates the world in six days, then forms a man from dust. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: This book is divided into sections by the repeated phrase “These are the generations of,” and it ends with a man dying in Egypt at age 110 after making his brothers promise to carry his bones to Canaan.
tossups.r: That man was Joseph, whose brothers had once sold him. For 10 points, name this first book of the Torah, which begins with creation.

tossups.p: This book says that Enoch “walked with God” and then was gone, because God took him, and that Enoch’s son Methuselah [“meh-THOO-zuh-luh”] lived 969 years, longer than anyone else in the Bible. This book also briefly mentions mighty beings called the Nephilim [“NEF-ih-lim”].
tossups.r: Methuselah’s grandson Noah builds an ark in this book. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, a man sends out a raven that keeps flying back and forth, then a dove that returns the second time with a freshly plucked olive leaf. His vessel had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat [“AIR-uh-rat”].
tossups.r: God then sets a rainbow in the sky as a sign of his covenant with that man, Noah. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, people settle in the land of Shinar [“SHY-nar”], bake bricks, and use tar for mortar to build a city with a tower reaching toward the heavens, until God confuses their language and scatters them across the earth.
tossups.r: That tower is known as the Tower of Babel. For 10 points, name this book that also tells the story of Noah’s ark.

tossups.p: In this book, a man uses a stone as a pillow and dreams of angels going up and down a stairway to heaven, so he names the place Bethel [“BETH-el”], meaning “house of God.” Years later, after wrestling with a stranger all night, he is renamed Israel.
tossups.r: That man is Jacob, the twin brother of Esau. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: On Ash Wednesday, many Christians receive ashes on their foreheads while hearing words that echo this book: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” In this book, God makes garments of animal skins for a couple before sending them out of their home.
tossups.r: That couple, Adam and Eve, had eaten fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, a prisoner explains that a ruler’s dream of seven thin cows swallowing seven fat cows means seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and the ruler puts him in charge of storing grain.
tossups.r: That prisoner, Joseph, had been sold into slavery by his brothers. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, a governor of Egypt has his silver cup hidden in the grain sack of his youngest brother, Benjamin, to test whether his other brothers have changed. Those brothers had once sold the governor to traders for twenty pieces of silver.
tossups.r: That governor, Joseph, is famous for his coat of many colors. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: Michelangelo painted nine scenes from this book down the center of the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512. Those panels begin with _The Separation of Light from Darkness_. Joseph Haydn drew on this book’s opening chapters for a famous oratorio.
tossups.r: The most famous of Michelangelo’s scenes shows God giving life to Adam. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, two angels urge a man to leave, and he and his family flee to the small town of Zoar [“ZOH-ar”] as burning sulfur rains down on two wicked cities, but his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
tossups.r: Those cities were Sodom and Gomorrah. For 10 points, name this book, which also tells of Abraham and Isaac.

tossups.p: In this book, a hungry hunter sells his birthright to his twin brother for a bowl of red lentil stew, and that brother later wears goatskins on his hands and neck to trick their nearly blind father into blessing him.
tossups.r: Those twins were Esau and Jacob, and Jacob later married the sisters Leah and Rachel. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

clues.t: First book of the Bible, the Torah, and the Old Testament; it has 50 chapters
Opens with God creating the world in six days and resting on the seventh: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth”
Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden and are sent out
Noah builds an ark to survive the Flood
Tells the stories of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of Joseph
Cain kills his brother Abel, then asks God, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The Tower of Babel: God confuses the builders’ language and scatters them
After the Flood, God sets a rainbow in the sky as a sign of his covenant; the ark lands on the mountains of Ararat
Esau sells his birthright to his twin, Jacob, for lentil stew; Jacob tricks their father, Isaac, into blessing him
Jacob dreams of a stairway to heaven at Bethel and is renamed Israel after wrestling all night
Joseph, with his coat of many colors, is sold by his brothers, then rises to power in Egypt
Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed; Lot flees to Zoar, but his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt
God tests Abraham, who nearly sacrifices Isaac before an angel stops him
Its Hebrew name is its first word, meaning “in the beginning”; its Greek name means “origin”
Apollo 8’s crew read its first ten verses while orbiting the Moon on Christmas Eve 1968
John Steinbeck’s _East of Eden_ (1952) retells Cain and Abel and debates the Hebrew word timshel, “thou mayest”
A river from Eden splits into four: the Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates; cherubim guard the way to the tree of life
Documentary hypothesis: scholars see older sources such as J and P woven together, giving two creation stories (chapters 1 and 2)
Divided into sections by the repeated phrase “These are the generations of”
Methuselah lives 969 years; his father, Enoch, “walked with God” and was taken; the Nephilim are mentioned
Noah sends out a raven and a dove; the dove returns with a freshly plucked olive leaf
Babel’s builders in the land of Shinar use bricks and tar
Laban tricks Jacob into marrying Leah before Rachel; Jacob works seven more years for Rachel
Joseph explains Pharaoh’s dream of seven fat and seven thin cows: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine
Joseph has a silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack; his brothers had sold him for twenty pieces of silver
Michelangelo painted nine of its scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–1512); Haydn drew on it for his oratorio _The Creation_
Ends with Joseph’s death in Egypt at age 110, after he makes his brothers promise to carry his bones to Canaan
God tells Adam, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” words echoed on Ash Wednesday; God makes garments of skins for the couple

trap.title: First book, not the Torah
trap.body: Genesis is only the first of the five books of the Torah, so answering “Torah,” “Pentateuch,” or “Old Testament” names the whole collection, not this book. Clues about Moses, the burning bush, the ten plagues, and the Red Sea belong to the next book, Exodus, and Joseph’s story, which ends with his family settled in Egypt, is the bridge between them.
trap.fix: Creation, Eden, Cain and Abel, Noah, Babel, Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph mean Genesis; Moses, Pharaoh’s plagues, and Mount Sinai mean Exodus. Say “Genesis” (its Hebrew name, Bereshit, also works).
trap.line: Real answer line: Genesis (or Bereshit; accept First Book of Moses)

topics.name: Islam
topics.kicker: Faith of the Quran and the Prophet Muhammad · World’s second-largest religion
topics.dates: Began in Arabia in the 600s CE
topics.briefing: Five times a day, a call to prayer rings out from the towers of mosques, and Muslims around the world turn toward the Kaaba in Mecca to pray. Islam, whose name means “submission” to God, teaches that there is one God (Allah in Arabic) and that Muhammad was God’s final prophet. With about two billion followers, it is the world’s second-largest religion, and its believers follow the Five Pillars, from daily prayer to the pilgrimage called the Hajj.
topics.answerHtml: Islam (accept word forms like Muslims or the Islamic faith; do not accept a single branch such as “Sunni” or “Shia”; do not accept “Nation of Islam”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the day of Ashura [“AH-shoo-rah”], members of one branch of this religion mourn Husayn [“hoo-SAYN”], a grandson of its final prophet, who was killed with his small band of followers at the Battle of Karbala [“KAR-buh-luh”] in 680 CE. That branch believes Husayn’s father, Ali, should have been the community’s first leader.
tossups.r: That branch is Shia; the larger branch is Sunni. For 10 points, name this religion whose final prophet, its followers believe, was Muhammad.

tossups.p: Each prayer in this religion is made up of units called rak’ahs [“RAK-ahz”], which include bowing and touching the forehead to the ground. Before praying, followers wash their hands, face, arms, and feet in a ritual called wudu [“woo-DOO”], and the day’s required prayers run from Fajr [“FAJ-er”] at dawn to Isha [“ih-SHAH”] at night.
tossups.r: Those five daily prayers, called salat, are one of its Five Pillars. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers pray facing Mecca.

tossups.p: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman [“ooth-MAHN”], and Ali are honored as the four “Rightly Guided” caliphs [“KAY-lifs”] by this religion’s largest branch. After Ali’s death in 661, the Umayyad [“oo-MY-ad”] family took control of the caliphate and ruled from Damascus.
tossups.r: The caliphs were seen as successors to the Prophet Muhammad. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Quran.

tossups.p: According to this religion’s tradition, the angel Israfil [“iz-rah-FEEL”] will blow a trumpet to announce the Day of Judgment, and two angels named Munkar [“MOON-kar”] and Nakir [“nah-KEER”] question each person in the grave. Belief in angels is one of its six articles of faith, along with belief in God’s prophets and holy books.
tossups.r: Its followers believe the angel Gabriel revealed the Quran to Muhammad. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: A niche called a mihrab [“MIH-rahb”] shows worshippers which way to face in this religion’s houses of worship, and on Fridays a preacher gives a sermon from a stepped pulpit called a minbar. Five times a day, a man called a muezzin [“moo-EZ-in”] chants the call to prayer, or adhan [“ah-THAHN”], from a tall tower.
tossups.r: Those towers are minarets, and those buildings are mosques. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers face Mecca to pray.

tossups.p: Years in this religion’s calendar are often marked AH, for the Latin words Anno Hegirae [“AN-oh heh-JY-ree”], because that calendar counts from the year 622 CE. It follows the moon, so its year is only about 354 days long, and its holy month of fasting moves through all the seasons over time.
tossups.r: Year one is the year of the Hijra, when Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: According to this religion’s teachings, God sent earlier scriptures, including the Tawrat [“tow-RAHT”] to Moses, the Zabur [“zah-BOOR”] to David, and the Injil [“in-JEEL”] to Jesus, whom its followers honor as a prophet named Isa [“EE-sah”]. This religion calls Jews and Christians “People of the Book.”
tossups.r: Its followers believe its final scripture, the Quran, was revealed to Muhammad. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion whose savings stay above a set minimum for a full lunar year are expected to give a share, usually 2.5 percent, to the poor and others in need. That required charity is called zakat [“zuh-KAHT”], and many believers choose to pay it during their holy month of fasting.
tossups.r: Zakat is one of the Five Pillars, along with the Shahada and daily prayer. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers fast during Ramadan.

tossups.p: The poet Rumi [“ROO-mee”] belonged to a mystical movement within this religion, and after his death his followers in Konya [“KOHN-yah”], Turkey, founded the Mevlevi [“MEV-leh-vee”] order, whose members spin in a prayerful dance as “whirling dervishes.” That mystical movement is called Sufism.
tossups.r: Sufis seek a close, personal experience of God, whom followers of this religion call Allah. For 10 points, name this religion of the Quran.

tossups.p: In 732 CE, Charles Martel’s Franks defeated an Umayyad [“oo-MY-ad”] army from Spain at the Battle of Tours [“TOOR”], stopping its advance into France. For centuries, rulers who followed this religion held much of Spain, where they built a vast house of worship in Córdoba [“KOR-doh-bah”] famous for its red-and-white striped arches.
tossups.r: Indonesia has more followers of this religion than any other country. For 10 points, name this religion whose final prophet, its followers believe, was Muhammad.

tossups.p: Most members of one branch of this religion are “Twelvers,” who believe that the twelfth of their imams [“ih-MAHMZ”] went into hiding in the 800s and will one day return as the Mahdi [“MAH-dee”]. Iran is the largest country where most people belong to that branch, which honors Ali as the first imam.
tossups.r: That branch is Shia, and the larger branch is Sunni. For 10 points, name this religion that follows the teachings of Muhammad.

tossups.p: This religion’s name comes from an Arabic word meaning “submission” to God, and that word shares a root with salaam [“sah-LAHM”], meaning “peace.” Its followers often greet each other with the words “as-salamu alaykum” [“ah-sah-LAH-moo ah-LAY-koom”], meaning “peace be upon you.”
tossups.r: Its declaration of faith, the Shahada, says there is no god but God and that Muhammad is God’s messenger. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion eat food that is halal [“hah-LAHL”], meaning “permitted,” and avoid foods and drinks that are haram [“hah-RAHM”], or “forbidden,” such as pork and alcohol. When an animal is killed for halal meat, God’s name is traditionally spoken.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers fast from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan.

tossups.p: Before the special morning prayer of one festival of this religion, held on the first day of the month of Shawwal [“shah-WAHL”], believers give a charity gift so that poor families can celebrate too. Another festival remembers Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice his son, and many families share the meat of a sacrificed animal with relatives, neighbors, and the poor.
tossups.r: Those festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, which falls during the Hajj. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: In 1924, the new Republic of Turkey abolished the office of caliph, a title that Ottoman sultans had claimed since 1517. Centuries earlier, Abbasid [“uh-BASS-id”] caliphs in Baghdad supported a House of Wisdom, where scholars translated Greek books into Arabic during this religion’s Golden Age.
tossups.r: The first caliphs led the community after the death of Muhammad. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Quran.

clues.t: Its followers regard Muhammad as God’s final prophet and believe the angel Gabriel revealed the Quran to him
Holy book: the Quran, which believers regard as the word of God revealed in Arabic
Strictly monotheistic: teaches that there is one God, called Allah in Arabic
The Five Pillars: Shahada (declaration of faith), salat (prayer), zakat (charity), sawm (fasting), and Hajj (pilgrimage)
The world’s second-largest religion, with about two billion followers; Indonesia has more of them than any other country
Two main branches: Sunni, the large majority, and Shia, who believe Muhammad’s cousin Ali should have been his first successor
The Hijra (622): Muhammad’s move from Mecca to Medina, year 1 of its lunar calendar; years are marked AH (Anno Hegirae)
House of worship: the mosque (masjid); a muezzin chants the call to prayer (adhan) from a tower called a minaret
Salat: five daily prayers facing the Kaaba in Mecca (the qibla), after a ritual washing called wudu
Believers fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan, which ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr
The Hajj: a pilgrimage to Mecca required once in a lifetime of all who are able; Eid al-Adha falls during it
Its name means “submission” to God and shares an Arabic root with salaam (“peace”)
Honors earlier prophets such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus (Isa); calls Jews and Christians “People of the Book”
On Ashura, Shia believers mourn Muhammad’s grandson Husayn, killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680
Most Shia are Twelvers, who await the return of a hidden twelfth imam, the Mahdi; Iran is the largest Shia-majority country
The four “Rightly Guided” (Rashidun) caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali
Later caliphs: the Umayyads ruled from Damascus, and the Abbasids from Baghdad, home of the House of Wisdom
Six articles of faith: belief in God, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgment, and God’s decree
Tradition says the angel Israfil will blow the trumpet of Judgment Day, and the angels Munkar and Nakir question the dead
Earlier scriptures it honors: the Tawrat (Torah) of Moses, the Zabur (Psalms) of David, and the Injil (Gospel) of Jesus
A mosque’s mihrab (a niche) shows the direction of Mecca; the Friday sermon is given from a pulpit called a minbar
Zakat: required charity, usually 2.5 percent of savings held for a full lunar year
Daily prayers run from Fajr (dawn) to Isha (night); each is made of units called rak’ahs, with bowing and prostration
Sufism is its mystical tradition; the poet Rumi’s followers in Konya founded the Mevlevi order of “whirling dervishes”
Charles Martel’s Franks halted an Umayyad army from Spain at the Battle of Tours (732); in Spain, Umayyad rulers built the Great Mosque of Córdoba
Halal (“permitted”) food rules; pork and alcohol are haram (“forbidden”)
Ottoman sultans claimed the title of caliph from 1517 until the Republic of Turkey abolished the caliphate in 1924

trap.title: Religion, not prophet
trap.body: Islam tossups are crowded with other answer lines: Muhammad, the Quran, Mecca, the Hajj, and Ramadan all get tossups of their own, and their clues pile up in the middle of an Islam question. Clues like “one branch of this religion” mourning Husayn tempt players to say “Shia,” but a single branch is not accepted when the question wants the whole faith. The Nation of Islam, an American movement once led by Elijah Muhammad, is a different answer line too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This religion” or “this faith” means Islam (or Muslims). “This prophet” means Muhammad, “this book” means the Quran, “this city” means Mecca, and “this month” means Ramadan. Say Sunni or Shia only when the question asks for “this branch” or “this sect.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Islam (accept word forms like Muslims; do not accept a single branch such as “Sunni” or “Shia”)

topics.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
topics.kicker: Mother of Jesus in the Gospels · Honored in Christianity and Islam
topics.briefing: In the Gospel of Luke, the angel Gabriel visits a young woman in Nazareth and tells her she will give birth to a son named Jesus, and she answers, “Let it be to me according to your word.” Christians honor Mary as the mother of Jesus, and Catholics and Orthodox Christians call her by titles like “Mother of God” and “Our Lady.” The Quran honors her too: one whole chapter is named Maryam, her Arabic name.
topics.answerHtml: Mary (or the Virgin Mary or Mary, mother of Jesus; accept Maryam, Madonna, or Our Lady; prompt on “mother of Jesus,” “Mother of God,” or “Theotokos”; do not accept “Mary Magdalene”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At the Council of Ephesus [“EF-uh-sus”] in 431 CE, church leaders approved calling this woman Theotokos [“thee-oh-TOH-kohs”], or “God-bearer,” rejecting the view of Nestorius [“neh-STOR-ee-us”], who preferred the title “Christ-bearer.” Cyril of Alexandria led the bishops who defended her title.
tossups.r: Catholic and Orthodox Christians often call her the Mother of God. For 10 points, name this woman whom Christians honor as the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: In the 1854 document _Ineffabilis Deus_ [“in-eh-FAH-bih-lees DAY-oos”], Pope Pius IX declared that this woman had been kept free from original sin from the moment she was conceived in her own mother’s womb. Catholics celebrate that teaching every year on December 8.
tossups.r: That teaching, the Immaculate Conception, is often confused with the virgin birth of her son. For 10 points, name this mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: In 1950, Pope Pius XII declared that at the end of her earthly life, this woman was taken up body and soul into heaven. Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate a related feast called the Dormition [“dor-MISH-un”], or “falling asleep,” and Titian [“TISH-un”] painted her rising into the sky in a huge altarpiece in Venice.
tossups.r: Catholics celebrate the Feast of the Assumption on August 15. For 10 points, name this mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: In December 1531, an Indigenous man named Juan Diego reported seeing this woman on Tepeyac [“teh-peh-YAHK”] Hill near Mexico City. According to the story, when he opened his cloak to show roses to Bishop Juan de Zumárraga [“soo-MAR-rah-gah”], her image appeared on the cloth.
tossups.r: That image is honored as the Virgin of Guadalupe. For 10 points, name this woman, the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: In 1858, fourteen-year-old Bernadette Soubirous [“soo-bee-ROO”] said that a lady appeared to her eighteen times in a grotto near a town in southwestern France. Millions of pilgrims visit that grotto, where many hope to be healed by water from its spring.
tossups.r: Bernadette said the lady told her, “I am the Immaculate Conception.” That town is Lourdes [“LOORD”]. For 10 points, name this mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: Three shepherd children, Lúcia [“LOO-see-ah”] dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, said this woman appeared to them several times in 1917 near a village in Portugal. Tens of thousands of people gathered there on October 13 of that year, and many reported seeing the “Miracle of the Sun.”
tossups.r: That village, Fátima [“FAH-tee-mah”], became one of the world’s great pilgrimage sites. For 10 points, name this mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: This woman told the servants, “Do whatever he tells you,” after she noticed that the hosts of a wedding feast had run out of wine. Her son then had the servants fill six stone jars with water, which became wine, and the Gospel of John calls this the first of his signs.
tossups.r: That wedding took place at Cana [“KAY-nuh”], in Galilee. For 10 points, name this woman, the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: After her relative Elizabeth greeted her as “blessed among women,” this woman sang a hymn of praise that begins, “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Johann Sebastian Bach and Claudio Monteverdi [“mon-teh-VAIR-dee”] both set that hymn, the Magnificat [“mag-NIF-ih-kaht”], to music.
tossups.r: Elizabeth was the mother of John the Baptist. For 10 points, name this woman who gave birth to Jesus.

tossups.p: Fra Angelico [“an-JEL-ih-koh”] and Leonardo da Vinci both painted an angel visiting this woman in Nazareth, where, according to the Gospel of Luke, she answered, “Let it be to me according to your word.” In older Catholic translations, the angel greets her with “Hail, full of grace,” words that begin a famous prayer.
tossups.r: Christians celebrate that visit by the angel Gabriel, the Annunciation, on March 25. For 10 points, name this mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: One chapter of the Quran, the only one named for a woman, says this woman gave birth beneath a palm tree and was told to shake its trunk so that ripe dates would fall for her. In that chapter, her newborn son speaks from the cradle to defend her when people accuse her of wrongdoing.
tossups.r: The Quran calls her son Isa and honors him as a prophet. For 10 points, name this woman, the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: The only work Michelangelo ever signed shows this woman with his name carved on a sash across her chest. In that marble sculpture in St. Peter’s Basilica, she sits holding the body of her son across her lap after the Crucifixion.
tossups.r: That sculpture is the _Pietà_ [“pee-ay-TAH”]. For 10 points, name this woman, the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: A medieval hymn that begins “Stabat Mater” [“STAH-baht MAH-ter”] describes this woman standing in sorrow at the foot of the cross. In the Gospel of John, her dying son tells her, “Woman, behold your son,” and tells his beloved disciple, “Behold your mother.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman, who stood by the cross of her son, Jesus.

tossups.p: When this woman and her husband presented their baby at the Temple in Jerusalem, a devout man named Simeon told her that “a sword will pierce your own soul too.” In the Gospel of Matthew, an angel warns her husband in a dream to take the family to Egypt to escape King Herod.
tossups.r: Her husband was Joseph, a carpenter from Nazareth. For 10 points, name this woman, the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: According to a second-century text called the Protoevangelium [“PROH-toh-ee-van-JEL-ee-um”] of James, this woman’s parents were named Joachim [“JOH-uh-kim”] and Anne, and she was raised in the Temple in Jerusalem. A huge Catholic basilica in Washington, D.C., honors her as patron saint of the United States.
tossups.r: That basilica is named for her Immaculate Conception. For 10 points, name this woman, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus.

tossups.p: In 2002, Pope John Paul II added five Luminous Mysteries to a prayer devotion honoring this woman, which already had Joyful, Sorrowful, and Glorious Mysteries. In that devotion, people count prayers on a string of beads in groups of ten called decades, and each of those prayers begins with the angel’s greeting to her.
tossups.r: That devotion and its beads are called the rosary. For 10 points, name this woman whom Catholics honor as the mother of Jesus.

clues.t: Mother of Jesus; the Gospels of Matthew and Luke say she conceived him while still a virgin
Wife of Joseph, a carpenter from Nazareth
Gave birth to Jesus in Bethlehem and laid him in a manger, because there was no room at the inn
The Annunciation: in Luke, the angel Gabriel tells her she will bear a son named Jesus
Immaculate Conception (declared by Pius IX in 1854): she herself was conceived free of original sin; feast on December 8
Assumption (declared by Pius XII in 1950): taken body and soul into heaven; feast on August 15 (the Orthodox Dormition)
At the wedding at Cana, she said “Do whatever he tells you,” and Jesus turned water into wine, his first sign in John
Sang the Magnificat (“My soul magnifies the Lord”) while visiting her relative Elizabeth; Bach and Monteverdi set it to music
Virgin of Guadalupe (1531): Juan Diego reported a vision on Tepeyac Hill near Mexico City; tradition says her image appeared on his cloak
Lourdes, France (1858): Bernadette Soubirous reported seeing a lady who said, “I am the Immaculate Conception”
Fátima, Portugal (1917): three shepherd children reported visions; crowds reported the “Miracle of the Sun” on October 13
The only woman named in the Quran; its 19th chapter (surah) bears her Arabic name
A famous Catholic prayer, said on rosary beads, begins with the angel’s greeting “Hail, full of grace”
The Council of Ephesus (431) called her Theotokos (“God-bearer”), rejecting Nestorius’s title “Christ-bearer”
Michelangelo’s _Pietà_ in St. Peter’s Basilica shows her holding her dead son; it is the only work he signed (on her sash)
The hymn “Stabat Mater” shows her grieving at the cross; in John, Jesus entrusts her to his beloved disciple (“Behold your mother”)
At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon told her that “a sword will pierce your own soul too”
In Matthew, an angel warns Joseph in a dream, and the family flees to Egypt to escape King Herod
The second-century Protoevangelium of James names her parents Joachim and Anne
Catholics honor her, under the title of the Immaculate Conception, as patron saint of the United States; a huge basilica in Washington, D.C., is named for that title
The Quran says she gave birth under a palm tree and shook it for dates; her newborn son spoke from the cradle to defend her
Titian painted her rising into heaven in a huge altarpiece in Venice
Fra Angelico and Leonardo da Vinci painted the Annunciation; in Luke she replies, “Let it be to me according to your word”
Rosary prayers are counted in decades; John Paul II added the Luminous Mysteries (2002) to the Joyful, Sorrowful, and Glorious

trap.title: Which Mary?
trap.body: The New Testament has several Marys. Mary Magdalene, a follower of Jesus, is the first to see him after his Resurrection in the Gospel of John, and Mary of Bethany is the sister of Martha and Lazarus; answering either one loses this tossup. Clues about her family also tempt early buzzes on Elizabeth, her relative; Anne, her mother in tradition; or Gabriel, the angel of the Annunciation.
trap.fix: Motherhood clues (the Annunciation, Bethlehem, Cana, the Pietà, the Magnificat) and apparitions such as Guadalupe, Lourdes, and Fátima mean the mother of Jesus. Remember that the Immaculate Conception (1854) is about her own conception without original sin, not about the birth of Jesus.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mary (or the Virgin Mary; accept Maryam; do not accept “Mary Magdalene”)

topics.name: Nirvana
topics.kicker: Buddhism’s highest goal · The “blowing out” of craving and rebirth
topics.briefing: Picture a candle flame going out: that is what the word nirvana means, a “blowing out.” Buddhists believe that greed, hatred, and delusion keep beings trapped in samsara, an endless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth, and that nirvana is the perfect peace that comes when those fires go out for good. According to tradition, Siddhartha Gautama reached it at about age 35, becoming the Buddha, and taught the Eightfold Path as the way there.
topics.answerHtml: nirvana (or nibbana; accept parinirvana; prompt on enlightenment, awakening, bodhi, or liberation; do not accept “moksha,” “samsara,” or “satori”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Fire Sermon, the Buddha taught that the eyes, the ears, and even the mind are “burning” with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, and T. S. Eliot named part of his poem _The Waste Land_ after that sermon. This state is reached when those three fires go out for good.
tossups.r: Its name is often translated as “blowing out,” like a flame. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, an escape from the cycle of rebirth.

tossups.p: At Kushinagar [“koo-shee-NAH-gar”] in India, the dying Buddha lay on his right side between two sal [“SAHL”] trees and told his monks, “All conditioned things pass away; strive on with diligence.” Giant reclining statues, like the one at Wat Pho [“waht POH”] in Bangkok, show him at the moment he entered the final form of this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of freedom from the cycle of rebirth, which Buddhists seek by following the Eightfold Path.

tossups.p: The philosopher Nagarjuna [“nah-GAR-joo-nuh”] argued that there is not the slightest difference between this state and samsara [“sum-SAH-ruh”], since both are “empty” of any fixed, independent existence. Nagarjuna founded the Middle Way, or Madhyamaka [“mahd-YAH-muh-kuh”], school of Mahayana Buddhism.
tossups.r: This state ends samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. For 10 points, name this ultimate goal of Buddhism.

tossups.p: When the wanderer Vacchagotta [“VAH-chuh-GOHT-tuh”] asked where an enlightened person goes after death, the Buddha asked him which way a fire goes when it goes out, to show that the question did not fit. A person who reaches this state while alive is said to have no fuel left for another birth.
tossups.r: Its Sanskrit name means “blowing out,” like a candle flame. For 10 points, name this Buddhist state of perfect peace.

tossups.p: A truth called nirodha [“nih-ROH-dah”], or “cessation,” teaches that suffering and the craving behind it can come to a complete end, and this state is that ending. The Buddha first taught that truth, the third of four, in his first sermon in the Deer Park at Sarnath [“SAR-naht”].
tossups.r: Those teachings are the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this goal of the Noble Eightfold Path.

tossups.p: Mahayana Buddhists honor bodhisattvas [“boh-dee-SAHT-vuhz”], such as Avalokiteshvara [“uh-vuh-loh-kih-TAYSH-vuh-ruh”], who put off their own final entry into this state in order to help all other beings reach it. In the Pure Land school, believers hope to be reborn in Amitabha’s [“uh-mee-TAH-buhz”] paradise, where reaching this state is easier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, often explained as the “blowing out” of craving.

tossups.p: Theravada Buddhism describes four stages on the way to this state, beginning with the “stream-enterer,” who is said to reach it within seven more lifetimes. The middle stages are the once-returner and the non-returner, and a person at the fourth stage, who has reached it, is called an arhat [“AR-hut”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state in which craving and suffering end, the ultimate goal of Buddhism.

tossups.p: Verses of the _Dhammapada_ [“DAH-muh-PAH-duh”] call this state “the highest happiness,” and another early text describes it as unborn and unconditioned. Unlike heaven in many religions, it is usually described not as a place but as a state of perfect peace that words cannot fully capture.
tossups.r: Buddhists believe it brings an end to rebirth. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, whose name means “blowing out.”

tossups.p: Jains celebrate Diwali as the night when Mahavira [“muh-HAH-vee-ruh”], the last of their twenty-four great teachers, reached this state at Pawapuri [“PAH-vah-poo-ree”] in eastern India. Jains often call the soul’s final liberation moksha, but they use this word for Mahavira’s passing too.
tossups.r: In Buddhism, it is the goal of the Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this state of liberation from rebirth.

tossups.p: Tibetan paintings of the Wheel of Life show a rooster, a snake, and a pig chasing each other at the center, standing for greed, hatred, and ignorance. The whole wheel, gripped by Yama [“YAH-muh”], the lord of death, stands for the cycle of rebirth, and a Buddha is often painted outside it, pointing the way to this state.
tossups.r: That cycle of rebirth is called samsara. For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, which frees a person from samsara forever.

tossups.p: Some Buddhist texts describe two kinds of this state: one “with remainder,” reached by an enlightened person who is still alive, and one “without remainder,” reached at that person’s death, when the five aggregates [“AG-reh-gits”] that make up a living being fall away for good.
tossups.r: Siddhartha Gautama reached it while meditating under the Bodhi tree, becoming the Buddha. For 10 points, name this state, which ends suffering and rebirth.

tossups.p: In one parable, the Buddha compared his teachings to a raft that carries a traveler across a river to the safety of the far shore, and said the raft should be left behind once the crossing is done. Buddhist texts often call this state “the further shore.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, a state of perfect peace beyond the cycle of rebirth.

tossups.p: Theravada monks practice vipassana [“vih-PAH-suh-nuh”], or “insight” meditation, hoping to see clearly that nothing lasts and that there is no unchanging self, an insight said to lead to this state. Right mindfulness and right concentration are the last two steps of the path to it.
tossups.r: That path is the Noble Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, an end to suffering and rebirth.

tossups.p: According to tradition, the demon Mara [“MAH-ruh”] sent armies and temptations to stop Siddhartha Gautama as he meditated at Bodh Gaya, but Siddhartha touched the earth to call it as his witness and then reached this state. He later taught a “Middle Way” between luxury and harsh self-denial that leads to this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, whose name comes from a Sanskrit word for “blowing out.”

tossups.p: After eating a final meal served by a metalworker named Cunda [“CHOON-dah”], the eighty-year-old Buddha fell ill, but he told his followers that Cunda should not be blamed. Soon afterward, the Buddha died and entered the final, complete form of this state.
tossups.r: In everyday English, its name has come to mean any state of perfect happiness. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism.

clues.t: The ultimate goal of Buddhism: freedom from suffering and from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth
Its Sanskrit name means “blowing out,” like a candle flame going out
Siddhartha Gautama reached it while meditating under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha (“Awakened One”)
Reached by following the Noble Eightfold Path
The third Noble Truth (nirodha, “cessation”): suffering can end, and this state is its ending
Reached when the three fires (or poisons) of greed, hatred, and delusion go out
In Theravada Buddhism, a person who has reached it is called an arhat (“worthy one”)
Mahayana bodhisattvas put off their own final entry into it in order to help all beings
The Buddha entered its final, complete form when he died at Kushinagar, at about age 80
Described not as a place like heaven but as a state of perfect peace beyond words
Tradition says Siddhartha resisted the demon Mara at Bodh Gaya before reaching it; he later taught a “Middle Way” between luxury and self-denial that leads to it
The Fire Sermon says the senses are “burning”; T. S. Eliot named part of _The Waste Land_ after it
Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, said there is not the slightest difference between it and samsara
Asked by Vacchagotta where an enlightened person goes after death, the Buddha asked which way a fire goes when it goes out
Reclining Buddha statues (like Wat Pho’s in Bangkok) show him dying on his right side; last words: “strive on with diligence”
Four stages to it: stream-enterer (within seven lives), once-returner, non-returner, and arhat
The _Dhammapada_ calls it “the highest happiness”; another early text describes it as unborn and unconditioned
Jains celebrate Diwali as the night Mahavira reached it at Pawapuri (Jains also call the soul’s final liberation moksha)
Tibetan Wheel of Life: a rooster, snake, and pig stand for greed, hatred, and ignorance; a Buddha outside the wheel points the way out
Two kinds: “with remainder” (while still alive) and “without remainder” (at death, when the five aggregates fall away)
The raft parable: the teachings carry you to the “further shore,” a name for this state, and are then left behind
Vipassana (“insight”) meditation, right mindfulness, and right concentration lead toward it
The Buddha fell ill after a last meal from the metalworker Cunda, then died and entered its final form
Pure Land Buddhists hope to be reborn in Amitabha’s paradise, where reaching it is easier

trap.title: Nirvana, moksha, or satori?
trap.body: Nirvana tossups are packed with words that sound like answers. Enlightenment (bodhi, or “awakening”) is the insight the Buddha gained under the Bodhi tree, and it earns only a prompt here. Moksha is the Hindu and Jain word for liberation, samsara is the cycle of rebirth that nirvana ends, and satori is a Zen word for a moment of awakening; none of those is accepted.
trap.fix: If the question describes a “blowing out,” the end of the three fires, the third Noble Truth, or what arhats and bodhisattvas reach, say nirvana. If you are prompted after saying “enlightenment,” add “nirvana”; save moksha for Hindu questions about Brahman and the atman.
trap.line: Real answer line: nirvana (or nibbana; prompt on enlightenment or bodhi; do not accept “moksha” or “samsara”)

topics.name: Quakers
topics.kicker: The Religious Society of Friends · Silent worship and a peace testimony
topics.briefing: In a traditional Quaker meeting for worship, there is no minister, no music, and no sermon: people sit together in silence until someone feels moved to speak. The Religious Society of Friends began in England in the 1650s with George Fox, who taught that there is “that of God in every one.” Quakers became known for refusing to fight in wars, for William Penn’s colony of Pennsylvania, and for helping lead the fight against slavery.
topics.answerHtml: Quakers (or Religious Society of Friends; accept word forms like Quakerism or Friends Church; prompt on Friends; do not accept “Shakers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1650, a judge in Derby named Gervase Bennet [“JER-vus BEN-it”] mocked this group with its best-known nickname after its founder told him to “tremble at the word of the Lord.” Early members of this group called themselves “Children of the Light.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox, known for its silent meetings for worship.

tossups.p: In 1652, this group’s founder climbed Pendle Hill in northern England and had a vision of “a great people to be gathered.” A few weeks later, he preached to about a thousand people on a hillside called Firbank Fell, an event often seen as this group’s true beginning.
tossups.r: That founder, George Fox, taught that there is “that of God in every one.” For 10 points, name this Christian group that worships in silence.

tossups.p: Margaret Fell, often called this group’s “mother,” made her home, Swarthmoor [“SWORTH-moor”] Hall, a center for its early traveling preachers, and she later married its founder. She wrote a 1666 pamphlet, _Women’s Speaking Justified_, defending the right of women to preach.
tossups.r: Her husband, George Fox, founded this group. For 10 points, name this Christian denomination known for its silent meetings.

tossups.p: Mary Dyer was hanged on Boston Common in 1660 for returning to Massachusetts Bay Colony after its Puritan leaders had banished her for belonging to this group. A statue of her stands outside the Massachusetts State House.
tossups.r: Puritan leaders opposed this group’s belief that God speaks to every person directly. For 10 points, name this group founded by George Fox.

tossups.p: While imprisoned in the Tower of London, a member of this group wrote _No Cross, No Crown_. In 1681, King Charles II paid off a debt owed to that writer’s father, an admiral, by granting the writer a huge tract of land in America.
tossups.r: That writer, William Penn, founded Pennsylvania as a “Holy Experiment” for this persecuted group. For 10 points, name this Christian group known for its silent worship.

tossups.p: Benjamin West painted a member of this group making a treaty with the Lenape [“leh-NAH-pay”] people beneath a great elm tree at Shackamaxon [“shack-uh-MAX-un”]. That man named his new colony’s capital Philadelphia, from Greek words meaning “brotherly love.”
tossups.r: That man, William Penn, belonged to this group. For 10 points, name this Christian group known for refusing to swear oaths.

tossups.p: In 1688, four members of this group in the settlement of Germantown signed one of the earliest written protests against slavery in the English colonies. In the next century, John Woolman traveled from meeting to meeting, urging fellow believers to free the people they enslaved.
tossups.r: This group became early leaders of the abolitionist movement. For 10 points, name this Christian group whose most famous colonist was William Penn.

tossups.p: Levi Coffin, nicknamed the “President of the Underground Railroad,” and Thomas Garrett, who helped Harriet Tubman in Wilmington, Delaware, both belonged to this religious group. In the 1700s, its members became some of the first Americans to forbid slaveholding among themselves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox, whose members worship in silent meetings.

tossups.p: The minister Lucretia Mott, who helped organize the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, belonged to this group, and Susan B. Anthony was raised in it. Alice Paul, who wrote the Equal Rights Amendment, also came from this group, which allowed women to preach from its earliest days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religious group that William Penn joined as a young man.

tossups.p: Elizabeth Fry, whose portrait appeared on the Bank of England’s five-pound note, worked to improve conditions for women prisoners at Newgate Prison as a member of this group. The families who founded the Cadbury and Rowntree chocolate companies also belonged to it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Christian group founded in England by George Fox, known for its silent worship.

tossups.p: In 1947, the Nobel Peace Prize went to two service committees, one based in London and one in Philadelphia, that represented this group. The American committee had been founded in 1917 so that conscientious objectors from this group could do relief work instead of fighting in World War I.
tossups.r: Members of this group follow a “peace testimony” against all war. For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox.

tossups.p: Herbert Hoover was born into this religious group in West Branch, Iowa, and Richard Nixon graduated from a college it founded in Whittier, California. That college was named for the abolitionist poet John Greenleaf Whittier, who also belonged to this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religious group, whose member William Penn founded Pennsylvania as a refuge for it.

tossups.p: This group’s founder dismissed church buildings as “steeplehouses,” and its members worship in plain meetinghouses with no altar. At business meetings, they make decisions without voting, as a member called the clerk waits for a shared “sense of the meeting.”
tossups.r: In many of its worship meetings, members sit in silence until someone feels moved to speak. For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox.

tossups.p: Early members of this group refused to take off their hats for judges or nobles and called everyone “thee” and “thou” to show that all people are equal. They also refused to swear oaths, and they traditionally called Sunday “First Day” to avoid day names with pagan roots.
tossups.r: A famous oatmeal brand named for this group has no ties to it. For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox.

tossups.p: Robert Barclay’s _Apology for the True Christian Divinity_ became the classic defense of this group’s beliefs, including the idea of an “Inward Light” in every person. In 1660, members of this group told King Charles II that they utterly rejected fighting “with outward weapons.”
tossups.r: Bayard Rustin, who organized the 1963 March on Washington, belonged to this pacifist group. For 10 points, name this Christian group founded by George Fox.

clues.t: Founded by George Fox in England in the mid-1600s
Known for silent worship: people sit quietly in a meetinghouse until someone feels moved to speak
William Penn, a member, founded Pennsylvania (1681) as a refuge for them, a “Holy Experiment”
Pacifists: their “peace testimony” rejects all war, and many have been conscientious objectors
Believe in an Inner (or Inward) Light, “that of God in every one,” so many meetings have no paid minister
Early leaders of abolition; Levi Coffin and Thomas Garrett helped freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad
