Women could preach from the start; Lucretia Mott helped organize Seneca Falls (1848), and Susan B. Anthony and Alice Paul grew up in the group
1947 Nobel Peace Prize to its British and American service committees (the American one was founded in 1917)
Plain speech: “thee” and “thou” for everyone, no hat-raising for nobles, no oaths, and “First Day” for Sunday
Penn named Philadelphia (“brotherly love”) and made a treaty with the Lenape, painted by Benjamin West
Presidents Herbert Hoover (born in West Branch, Iowa) and Richard Nixon (Whittier College) were raised in it
A famous oatmeal brand is named for the group but has no ties to it
Nickname from Judge Gervase Bennet (1650), after Fox told him to “tremble at the word of the Lord”; early name: “Children of the Light”
Fox’s 1652 vision on Pendle Hill of “a great people to be gathered”; he then preached at Firbank Fell
Margaret Fell, the movement’s “mother,” hosted preachers at Swarthmoor Hall, wrote _Women’s Speaking Justified_ (1666), and married Fox
Mary Dyer was hanged on Boston Common (1660) for returning to Puritan Massachusetts after being banished
Penn wrote _No Cross, No Crown_ in the Tower of London; Charles II granted him land to repay a debt to Penn’s father, an admiral
1688 Germantown petition: one of the earliest written protests against slavery in the English colonies
John Woolman traveled among meetings urging members to free the people they enslaved
Elizabeth Fry improved conditions for women prisoners at Newgate Prison and appeared on the five-pound note
The families who founded the Cadbury and Rowntree chocolate companies were members
Fox called churches “steeplehouses”; business meetings decide by the “sense of the meeting,” without voting, guided by a clerk
Robert Barclay’s _Apology for the True Christian Divinity_ was the classic defense of its beliefs
A 1660 declaration to Charles II rejected fighting “with outward weapons,” the root of its peace testimony
Bayard Rustin, who organized the 1963 March on Washington, was a member

trap.title: Quakers, not Shakers
trap.body: Several Protestant groups from England and colonial America get mixed up. The Shakers began as an offshoot nicknamed the “Shaking Quakers” and became famous for celibate communities, simple furniture, and the song “Simple Gifts.” The Puritans were the group that banished and hanged Quakers in Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania clues can tempt players to name the Amish or Mennonites, German-speaking groups who also settled there.
trap.fix: George Fox, William Penn, silent meetings, the Inner Light, “thee” and “thou,” and the 1947 Nobel Peace Prize mean the Quakers. Ann Lee and “Simple Gifts” mean the Shakers; Jakob Ammann and horse-drawn buggies mean the Amish; John Winthrop’s “city upon a hill” means the Puritans.
trap.line: Real answer line: Quakers (or Religious Society of Friends; accept Friends Church; do not accept “Shakers”)

topics.name: Quran
topics.kicker: Holy book of Islam · Muslims believe it was revealed to Muhammad
topics.dates: Revealed 610–632 CE, according to Muslim belief
topics.briefing: Muslims believe the Quran is the word of God, revealed in Arabic to the Prophet Muhammad by the angel Gabriel over about 23 years, starting in a mountain cave around 610. Its 114 chapters, called surahs, run roughly from longest to shortest, and its name means “the recitation.” Many Muslims memorize the entire book, earning the title hafiz, and printed copies are handled with great respect.
topics.answerHtml: Quran (or Koran or Qur’an; accept al-Quran or the Holy Quran; do not accept “Hadith” or “Sunnah”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The seven verses of this book’s opening chapter, “The Opening,” are recited in every unit of the daily prayers, and they ask God to “guide us to the straight path.” This book’s last two chapters, “The Daybreak” and “The People,” are often recited for protection.
tossups.r: That opening chapter is called al-Fatiha [“al-FAH-tee-hah”]. For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam.

tossups.p: Except for its short opening chapter, this book’s chapters are arranged roughly from longest to shortest, not in the order in which believers say they were revealed. The longest, “The Cow,” has 286 verses, while “Abundance,” or al-Kawthar [“al-KOW-thar”], has only three.
tossups.r: This book has 114 chapters, called surahs. For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam.

tossups.p: According to tradition, after many people who had memorized this book died at the Battle of Yamama [“yah-MAH-mah”], Abu Bakr asked Zayd ibn Thabit [“ZAYD ib-un THAH-bit”] to gather its verses from written pieces and from memory. Under the third caliph, Uthman [“ooth-MAHN”], an official standard text was copied and sent to major cities.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe was revealed to Muhammad.

tossups.p: A person who has memorized all of this book is honored with the title hafiz [“HAH-fiz”], and skilled reciters, called qaris [“KAH-reez”], follow detailed rules of pronunciation and rhythm called tajwid [“taj-WEED”] when they chant it aloud.
tossups.r: During Ramadan, many mosques recite one-thirtieth of it each night. For 10 points, name this scripture of Islam.

tossups.p: According to tradition, the first words of this book to be revealed open the chapter called “The Clot,” with the command “Read!” or “Recite!” in the name of God, who created humans from a clinging clot. Believers say those words came in a cave on Mount Hira [“hih-RAH”] around 610.
tossups.r: Muslims believe the angel Gabriel brought this book to Muhammad over about 23 years. For 10 points, name this scripture.

tossups.p: This book’s name comes from an Arabic word meaning “the recitation.” Because believers hold that its exact Arabic words came from God, translations into other languages are usually treated as interpretations of its meaning rather than as the book itself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, divided into 114 surahs.

tossups.p: A short chapter of this book says that the night on which it was first sent down is “better than a thousand months.” Believers mark that night, Laylat al-Qadr [“LAY-lat al-KAH-der”], or the Night of Power, during the last ten nights of a holy month.
tossups.r: That month is Ramadan, when many Muslims try to read all of it. For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam.

tossups.p: The Throne Verse, the 255th verse of this book’s longest chapter, describes a God who is never overtaken by sleep, with a throne that “extends over the heavens and the earth.” Many believers recite that verse, Ayat al-Kursi [“AH-yat al-KOOR-see”], for protection before going to sleep.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, whose longest chapter is called “The Cow.”

tossups.p: Every chapter of this book except the ninth begins with the words “In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” That phrase, the basmala [“BAHS-muh-lah”], is also said by many believers before meals and other everyday actions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book that Muslims believe God revealed to Muhammad, made up of chapters called surahs.

tossups.p: The only chapter of this book named for a woman tells of the birth of Jesus, and another chapter calls the life of Joseph “the most beautiful of stories.” Moses is named in this book more often than any other person.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book that Muslims believe the angel Gabriel revealed to Muhammad.

tossups.p: Scholars divide this book’s chapters into earlier “Meccan” ones, which are usually short and focus on faith in one God and the coming judgment, and later “Medinan” ones, which are longer and give rules for family life and the community.
tossups.r: Each of those chapters is called a surah. For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, whose verses are called ayat [“ah-YAHT”].

tossups.p: In 2015, two pages of this book’s text held by the University of Birmingham, written on animal skin, were radiocarbon-dated to between 568 and 645 CE, making them among the oldest copies known. Other early pages were found in 1972, hidden in a space under the roof of the Great Mosque of Sanaa [“sah-NAH”] in Yemen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, whose standard text was compiled under the caliph Uthman.

tossups.p: In 1143, Robert of Ketton made the first Latin translation of this book for Peter the Venerable, the abbot of Cluny [“KLOO-nee”]. Centuries later, Thomas Jefferson owned a copy of George Sale’s English translation of this book, first published in 1734.
tossups.r: In 2007, Keith Ellison, the first Muslim elected to Congress, used Jefferson’s copy at his ceremonial swearing-in. For 10 points, name this scripture of Islam.

tossups.p: Twenty-nine chapters of this book open with mysterious separate letters, such as “Alif, Lam, Mim” [“AH-lif, LAHM, MEEM”], whose meaning scholars have long debated. Commentaries that explain this book’s meaning, such as a famous one by al-Tabari [“al-tah-BAH-ree”], are called tafsir [“taf-SEER”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, made up of 114 surahs.

tossups.p: This book challenges anyone who doubts it to produce even one chapter like it, and many believers regard its language as impossible to imitate. Out of respect, many believers wash before touching a printed copy of it and keep it on a high shelf, never on the floor.
tossups.r: Its 114 chapters are called surahs. For 10 points, name this holy book of Islam, whose name means “the recitation.”

clues.t: The holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe is the word of God
Muslims believe the angel Gabriel revealed it to Muhammad over about 23 years, beginning around 610
Divided into 114 chapters called surahs, made up of verses called ayat
Written in Arabic; its name means “the recitation”
Opens with al-Fatiha (“The Opening”), seven verses recited in every unit of daily prayer
Chapters run roughly from longest to shortest; “The Cow” (al-Baqarah, 286 verses) is the longest
A hafiz has memorized the whole book; skilled reciters (qaris) follow rules called tajwid
Believed to have been first sent down on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, in Ramadan; a short chapter calls that night “better than a thousand months”
Tradition says Zayd ibn Thabit collected it under Abu Bakr; a standard text was made under the third caliph, Uthman
Tradition says the first revealed words were “Read!” in a cave on Mount Hira; they open the chapter “The Clot”
Shortest chapter: al-Kawthar (“Abundance”), three verses; the last two chapters, “The Daybreak” and “The People,” are said for protection
Many memorizers died at the Battle of Yamama, which led to the first written collection
Translations are treated as interpretations, not the book itself, since believers hold that its Arabic words came from God
The Throne Verse (Ayat al-Kursi), verse 255 of “The Cow,” describes God’s throne over the heavens and the earth
Every chapter except the ninth begins with the basmala: “In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful”
Only chapter named for a woman: Maryam (Surah 19); Joseph’s story is “the most beautiful of stories”; Moses is named most often
Earlier Meccan chapters are short and about faith; later Medinan chapters are longer, with rules for the community
Birmingham pages radiocarbon-dated to 568–645 CE; early pages were also found in the Great Mosque of Sanaa, Yemen (1972)
First Latin translation by Robert of Ketton (1143); Jefferson owned George Sale’s English translation, which Keith Ellison used at his 2007 swearing-in
Twenty-nine chapters open with mysterious separate letters, like “Alif, Lam, Mim”
Tafsir: commentary explaining its meaning, such as al-Tabari’s
Challenges doubters to produce one chapter like it; believers wash before touching a copy and keep it on a high shelf
Divided into 30 parts, each called a juz’, so it can be recited over the nights of Ramadan

trap.title: Book, not sayings
trap.body: The Quran and the hadith are both central to Islam, but they are different answer lines. Muslims regard the Quran as God’s own words, revealed through Gabriel, while the hadith are reports of Muhammad’s sayings and actions, gathered later by scholars such as al-Bukhari. A question about a single chapter, like al-Fatiha or “The Cow,” may also want that chapter’s name instead of the whole book.
trap.fix: Surahs, ayat, a hafiz, Uthman’s standard text, or the first command “Read!” mean the Quran. Chains of narrators (isnad) or collections by al-Bukhari mean hadith; if the question says “this chapter,” give the surah’s name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Quran (or Koran or Qur’an; do not accept “Hadith”)

topics.name: Rosh Hashanah
topics.kicker: The Jewish New Year · Begins the Days of Awe with the shofar
topics.briefing: On Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, many families dip slices of apple in honey and wish each other a sweet year. In synagogue, worshippers hear the shofar, a trumpet made from a ram’s horn, sounded again and again. The two-day holiday falls on the first and second of Tishrei, in September or October, and begins the Days of Awe, ten days of reflection and repentance that end on Yom Kippur.
topics.answerHtml: Rosh Hashanah (or Rosh Hashana or other spellings; accept Jewish New Year or Yom Teruah; prompt on New Year or High Holy Days; do not accept “Yom Kippur”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A tractate of the Mishnah named for this holiday lists four different new years, including one for trees, celebrated as Tu BiShvat [“TOO bish-VAHT”], and one on the first day of Nisan [“nee-SAHN”] for counting the reigns of kings.
tossups.r: This holiday marks the new year for counting the years themselves. For 10 points, name this Jewish festival on the first two days of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”].

tossups.p: The Torah never calls this holiday by its usual name. Instead, Leviticus describes a day of rest on the first day of the seventh month, remembered with loud blasts, and the Book of Numbers calls it a “day of blowing.”
tossups.r: Those blasts are sounded on the shofar. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that celebrates the start of a new year in the fall.

tossups.p: This holiday’s additional, or Musaf [“MOO-sahf”], prayer service has three special sections: Malchuyot [“mahl-khoo-YOHT”], about God’s kingship; Zichronot [“zikh-roh-NOHT”], about remembrance; and Shofarot [“shoh-fah-ROHT”]. Each section includes ten verses from the Hebrew Bible and is followed by blasts of a ram’s horn.
tossups.r: That horn is the shofar. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday held on the first of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”].

tossups.p: On the second day of this holiday, synagogues read the Binding of Isaac, in which Abraham sacrifices a ram caught by its horns in a thicket instead of his son. On the first day, they read about Isaac’s birth and hear the prayer of Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel.
tossups.r: That ram is one reason a ram’s horn, the shofar, is blown on this holiday. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that starts the new year.

tossups.p: The prayer Unetanneh Tokef [“oo-neh-TAH-neh TOH-kef”] imagines all people passing before God like sheep before a shepherd as each one’s fate is decided: “who shall live and who shall die.” Tradition says that on this holiday, God opens books that record every person’s deeds.
tossups.r: Fates are said to be written on this holiday and sealed on Yom Kippur. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday.

tossups.p: On the afternoon of this holiday, many Jews walk to a river, lake, or ocean and toss bread crumbs into the water in a ceremony called Tashlich [“TAHSH-likh”]. The ceremony takes its name from a verse of Micah [“MY-kuh”] that says God will “cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that begins the Days of Awe leading up to Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: Some families eat the head of a fish on this holiday, hoping to be “the head and not the tail” in the coming year, and many eat pomegranates, whose many seeds stand for good deeds. Its challah [“KHAH-luh”] bread is usually baked in a round, spiral shape to show the circle of the year.
tossups.r: Many families also dip apples in honey for a sweet year. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that begins the new year.

tossups.p: A long blast called tekiah [“teh-KEE-ah”], three broken blasts called shevarim [“sheh-vah-REEM”], and nine short blasts called teruah [“teh-ROO-ah”] are sounded in set patterns on this holiday, ending with an extra-long tekiah gedolah [“teh-KEE-ah geh-doh-LAH”].
tossups.r: Those blasts come from a ram’s horn, the shofar. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday on the first of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”].

tossups.p: People greet each other on this holiday with “L’shanah tovah tikatevu” [“leh-shah-NAH toh-VAH tee-kah-TAY-voo”], meaning “May you be written down for a good year.” Worshippers also chant Avinu Malkeinu [“ah-VEE-noo mahl-KAY-noo”], a prayer whose name means “Our Father, Our King.”
tossups.r: This holiday begins the Ten Days of Repentance. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday celebrated with apples and honey.

tossups.p: Jewish tradition holds that this holiday marks the anniversary of the creation of Adam and Eve on the sixth day of creation, and one of its prayers calls it “the birthday of the world.” Its other names include the Day of Judgment and the Day of Remembrance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that starts the year with the sound of the shofar.

tossups.p: During most of the month of Elul [“eh-LOOL”] before this holiday, many synagogues sound a ram’s horn after weekday morning prayers. In the days just before it, many communities also gather to recite special prayers for forgiveness called selichot [“slee-KHOHT”].
tossups.r: This holiday falls on the first of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”]. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday, the first of the High Holy Days.

tossups.p: Unlike most Jewish festivals, this holiday lasts two days even in Israel, where its two days are treated as “one long day.” If its first day falls on the Sabbath, the ram’s horn is not sounded that day.
tossups.r: The Fast of Gedaliah [“ged-uh-LYE-uh”] usually comes the day after it ends. For 10 points, name this two-day Jewish holiday that begins the Days of Awe.

tossups.p: This holiday is the only major Jewish festival that falls on the first day of a month, at the new moon. The rabbis connected it to a psalm that tells the people to blow the horn at the new moon, on their feast day.
tossups.r: That horn is the shofar, and that month is Tishrei. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that comes about ten days before Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: The Hebrew calendar’s year number goes up by one on this holiday; for example, the year 5785 began on it in October 2024. Jewish tradition counts those years from the creation of the world described in Genesis.
tossups.r: This holiday falls on the first two days of Tishrei. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday celebrated with apples dipped in honey.

tossups.p: Many Sephardic [“seh-FAR-dik”] families hold a short seder on this holiday’s first night with symbolic foods such as leeks, beets, and dates. Each food is followed by a blessing that begins “May it be Your will,” often based on a pun on the food’s Hebrew or Aramaic name.
tossups.r: Families everywhere also dip apples in honey for a sweet year. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday of the new year.

clues.t: The new year festival of Judaism, celebrated in the fall
The shofar, a trumpet made from a ram’s horn, is sounded many times in synagogue
Families dip apples in honey to wish for a sweet new year
Falls on the 1st and 2nd of Tishrei, in September or October
Begins the Days of Awe (the Ten Days of Repentance), which end on Yom Kippur
Tashlich: tossing bread crumbs into flowing water to symbolize casting away sins, from a verse of Micah
Tradition: each person’s fate is written in the Book of Life on this day and sealed on Yom Kippur
Greeting: “L’shanah tovah” (“for a good year”), or in full, “May you be written down for a good year”
Round challah (the circle of the year), pomegranates (many good deeds), and fish heads (“the head and not the tail”)
Kept for two days, even in Israel; the first of the two High Holy Days
Torah readings: Isaac’s birth (day 1) and the Binding of Isaac, where a ram takes Isaac’s place (day 2)
A Mishnah tractate named for it lists four new years, including Tu BiShvat (trees) and the first of Nisan (kings)
Leviticus: a day of rest with loud blasts on the first day of the seventh month; the Book of Numbers calls it a “day of blowing”
Its Musaf service has three sections: Malchuyot (kingship), Zichronot (remembrance), and Shofarot
The first day’s reading from the prophets is the prayer of Hannah, mother of Samuel
Unetanneh Tokef: “who shall live and who shall die,” as all people pass before God like sheep
Shofar calls: tekiah (long), shevarim (three broken), teruah (nine short), and tekiah gedolah (extra-long)
Worshippers chant Avinu Malkeinu (“Our Father, Our King”)
Tradition says it marks the creation of Adam and Eve, “the birthday of the world”; also called the Day of Judgment and the Day of Remembrance
Preceded by the month of Elul, with weekday shofar blasts and selichot (prayers for forgiveness)
No shofar is sounded if the first day falls on the Sabbath; the Fast of Gedaliah usually comes the day after
The only major festival on the first of a month (the new moon); linked to a psalm about blowing the horn at the new moon
The Hebrew year number rises by one (5785 began in October 2024), counting from creation
Sephardic families hold a seder of symbolic foods (leeks, beets, dates), each with a “May it be Your will” blessing

trap.title: New Year or Atonement?
trap.body: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are the two High Holy Days, about ten days apart in the month of Tishrei, and they share the shofar, the Book of Life, and the Days of Awe that link them. Tradition says each person’s fate is written on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur, so buzzing on a Book of Life clue alone is risky. The Torah’s own name for this holiday, Yom Teruah (“day of blowing”), is accepted too.
trap.fix: Apples and honey, Tashlich, round challah, the Binding of Isaac reading, and many shofar blasts mean Rosh Hashanah. The 25-hour fast, Kol Nidre, Ne’ila, the Book of Jonah, and the scapegoat mean Yom Kippur. “New Year” or “High Holy Days” alone only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Rosh Hashanah (accept Jewish New Year or Yom Teruah; prompt on High Holy Days; do not accept “Yom Kippur”)

topics.name: Baptism
topics.kicker: Christian rite of initiation with water · Jesus was baptized in the Jordan
topics.briefing: According to the Gospels, Jesus waded into the Jordan River to be baptized by John the Baptist, and the Holy Spirit came down on him like a dove. Ever since, Christians have used baptism, a ritual washing with water, to welcome people into the church. Some churches baptize babies by pouring or sprinkling water, while others, like the Baptists, baptize only people old enough to profess their faith, often by dipping them completely under water.
topics.answerHtml: baptism (accept word forms like baptizing; accept christening; prompt on sacrament or immersion; do not accept “Baptists,” “Anabaptists,” or “confirmation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: An early Christian guidebook called the _Didache_ [“DID-uh-kay”] says this rite should be done in “living,” or running, water, but allows other water if there is none, and pouring water on the head three times as a last resort. It also says the person about to receive this rite should fast for a day or two beforehand.
tossups.r: John the Baptist performed this rite on Jesus in the Jordan River. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament of initiation.

tossups.p: Each January, Greek Orthodox teenagers in Tarpon Springs, Florida, dive into a bayou to retrieve a cross thrown into the water during Theophany [“thee-OFF-uh-nee”], a feast that celebrates the day Jesus received this rite. At that moment, according to the Gospels, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son.”
tossups.r: John the Baptist performed this rite on Jesus. For 10 points, name this Christian ritual of washing with water.

tossups.p: In January 1525, Conrad Grebel performed this rite on George Blaurock [“BLOU-rock”] at a house in Zurich, even though both men had already received it as babies. Members of the movement they started, called the Swiss Brethren, were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.
tossups.r: Their enemies called them Anabaptists, meaning people who repeat this rite. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament performed with water.

tossups.p: In 1609, the English pastor John Smyth, living in exile in Amsterdam, performed this rite on himself and then on his followers, rejecting the version he had received as an infant. His partner Thomas Helwys [“HEL-wiss”] later founded the first church of their denomination in England, in London.
tossups.r: That denomination, the Baptists, takes its name from this rite. For 10 points, name this Christian rite performed with water.

tossups.p: In 1638, Roger Williams founded the first church in the American colonies to perform this rite only on believers rather than on babies, in Providence. Williams himself left that church within a few months, but the congregation lives on in Rhode Island.
tossups.r: That congregation was the first Baptist church in America. For 10 points, name this rite, which many Baptists perform by dipping a person fully under water.

tossups.p: John Gadsby Chapman’s painting in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda shows Pocahontas receiving this rite, along with the new name Rebecca. In 988, Prince Vladimir of Kiev received it and then ordered the people of his city into the Dnieper [“NEE-per”] River to receive it too.
tossups.r: The Roman emperor Constantine waited until he was dying to receive it. For 10 points, name this Christian rite of washing with water.

tossups.p: Eastern Orthodox priests usually perform this rite by dipping a person in water three times, once for each person of the Trinity. Other churches perform it by affusion [“uh-FYOO-zhun”], or pouring water over the head, or by aspersion [“uh-SPUR-zhun”], or sprinkling.
tossups.r: Baptists usually perform it by full immersion. For 10 points, name this Christian rite of initiation.

tossups.p: Catholics teach that this sacrament washes away original sin, and in an emergency they allow anyone, even a person who is not a Christian, to perform it by using water and the right words. Godparents often make promises on behalf of a baby receiving it.
tossups.r: Catholics count it as the first of their seven sacraments. For 10 points, name this rite, which many churches give to babies.

tossups.p: At the end of the Gospel of Matthew, the risen Jesus tells his followers to make disciples of all nations and to perform this rite “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” That command is called the Great Commission.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Christian rite, which John the Baptist performed in the Jordan River.

tossups.p: In his Letter to the Romans, Paul says that believers who receive this rite are “buried with” Christ so that they can “walk in newness of life.” In the Gospel of John, Jesus tells Nicodemus [“nik-uh-DEE-mus”] that no one can enter the kingdom of God without being “born of water and the Spirit.”
tossups.r: Many churches teach that it marks a spiritual rebirth. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament performed with water.

tossups.p: In the Book of Acts, about three thousand people receive this rite on the day of Pentecost after Peter tells the crowd to repent. Later in that book, Philip performs it on an Ethiopian official, who asks, “Look, here is water! What can stand in the way?”
tossups.r: Christians see it as the way a person joins the church. For 10 points, name this rite that John the Baptist performed on Jesus.

tossups.p: Lorenzo Ghiberti made bronze doors nicknamed the “Gates of Paradise” for a building in Florence set aside for this rite. Leonardo da Vinci painted one of the angels in his teacher Andrea del Verrocchio’s [“vair-ROH-kee-ohz”] painting of Jesus receiving it.
tossups.r: In that scene, John the Baptist performs this rite on Jesus as a dove comes down from heaven. For 10 points, name this Christian rite.

tossups.p: Members of the small Mandaean [“man-DEE-un”] religion of Iraq and Iran repeat this rite often throughout their lives, always in flowing water. In Judaism, a similar ritual immersion takes place in a pool called a mikveh [“MIK-vuh”], which converts enter as part of joining the faith.
tossups.r: Mandaeans honor John the Baptist, who performed this rite on Jesus. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament.

tossups.p: The Salvation Army and the Quakers do not perform this water rite, which Quakers understand as an inward, spiritual experience instead. Latter-day Saints perform it on children at age eight and also perform it in their temples on behalf of ancestors who have died.
tossups.r: Most churches see it as the first step in Christian life. For 10 points, name this rite that John the Baptist performed.

tossups.p: Tertullian [“tur-TUL-yun”] wrote the oldest surviving essay devoted to this rite around 200 CE, and the Nicene Creed says that Christians acknowledge “one” such rite “for the forgiveness of sins.” Augustine argued against the Donatists [“DOH-nuh-tists”] that it should not be repeated, even if an unworthy priest had performed it.
tossups.r: Most churches perform it only once in a person’s life. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament, which Jesus received from John the Baptist.

clues.t: In the Gospels, John the Baptist performs it on Jesus in the Jordan River, and the Holy Spirit comes down like a dove
Christian rite of initiation with water, done by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling
Infant or believer’s: many churches give it to babies, while Baptists give it only to people who profess their faith
One of the two sacraments most Protestants keep (with communion), and the first of the seven Catholic sacraments
The Great Commission (end of Matthew): make disciples of all nations, “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”
The Gospels say that at Jesus’s, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son”; Eastern churches celebrate it at Theophany (Epiphany)
Three methods: immersion (dipping), affusion (pouring), and aspersion (sprinkling); the Orthodox immerse three times
Anabaptists (“re-doers” of it) began in Zurich in 1525, when Conrad Grebel performed it on George Blaurock
The Baptist denomination began with John Smyth in Amsterdam (1609); Thomas Helwys founded the first Baptist church in England
Catholics teach it washes away original sin; in an emergency anyone may perform it; godparents make promises for babies
The _Didache_ calls for “living” (running) water but allows pouring water on the head three times as a last resort; candidates fast a day or two first
At Tarpon Springs, Florida, Greek Orthodox teens dive for a cross each January on Theophany
Roger Williams founded the first Baptist church in America, in Providence, Rhode Island (1638)
Pocahontas received it and the name Rebecca (Chapman’s painting in the Capitol); Vladimir of Kiev in 988; Constantine on his deathbed
Paul says believers are “buried with” Christ in it; Jesus tells Nicodemus one must be “born of water and the Spirit”
In Acts, about 3,000 people receive it at Pentecost, and Philip performs it on an Ethiopian official
Ghiberti’s “Gates of Paradise” are on Florence’s building for this rite; Leonardo painted an angel in Verrocchio’s painting of Jesus receiving it
The Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran repeat it often in flowing water; Jewish converts immerse in a pool called a mikveh
The Quakers and the Salvation Army do not practice it with water; Latter-day Saints perform it at age 8 and for ancestors
Tertullian wrote the oldest surviving essay on it (c. 200); the Nicene Creed acknowledges just one “for the forgiveness of sins”
Augustine told the Donatists it should not be repeated, even if an unworthy priest had performed it

trap.title: Rite, not the Baptist
trap.body: Baptism shares its root with three other answer lines: John the Baptist, the prophet who performed it on Jesus; the Baptists, a Protestant denomination begun by John Smyth in 1609; and the Anabaptists, the 1525 movement whose heirs include the Mennonites and the Amish. Players also confuse it with confirmation, a later sacrament in which a baptized person affirms the faith, and with the Eastern Orthodox chrismation, an anointing with oil.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this rite,” “this sacrament,” or “this ritual,” answer baptism. Say Baptists only for “this denomination” and John the Baptist only for “this prophet” or “this man.” A bishop laying on hands or anointing with oil points to confirmation or chrismation.
trap.line: Real answer line: baptism (accept word forms like baptizing; accept christening; do not accept “Baptists” or “confirmation”)

topics.name: Scientology
topics.kicker: Religious movement founded by L. Ron Hubbard · First church opened in 1954
topics.briefing: In 1950, the science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard published _Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health_, which became a bestseller. Hubbard went on to found Scientology, and the first Church of Scientology opened in Los Angeles in 1954. Scientologists believe that each person is a thetan, an immortal spiritual being, and they seek spiritual improvement through one-on-one counseling sessions called auditing.
topics.answerHtml: Scientology (or Church of Scientology; accept word forms like Scientologists; prompt on Dianetics; do not accept “Christian Science”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In May 1950, the magazine _Astounding Science Fiction_, edited by John W. Campbell, published an article introducing a method of mental self-improvement that later grew into this movement. That same month, the article’s author published a bestselling book subtitled _The Modern Science of Mental Health_.
tossups.r: That book was _Dianetics_, by L. Ron Hubbard. For 10 points, name this religious movement that Hubbard founded.

tossups.p: Adherents of this religion believe that each person is a thetan [“THAY-tun”], an immortal spiritual being that is a person’s true self, separate from the body and the mind. They believe a thetan has lived many past lives and can be weighed down by painful experiences from this life and earlier ones.
tossups.r: Its first church opened in Los Angeles in 1954. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: In this religion’s central practice, a trained counselor asks a person questions while watching a device called an E-meter, which measures small changes in electrical resistance as the person holds two metal cylinders. That one-on-one counseling is called auditing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard, the author of _Dianetics_.

tossups.p: This movement’s founder taught that painful experiences leave mental image pictures called engrams [“EN-gramz”] in a part of the mind he called the reactive mind. Adherents believe that a person who has gotten rid of the reactive mind reaches a state called Clear.
tossups.r: Those ideas first appeared in the book _Dianetics_. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: After reaching the state called Clear, members of this religion may move on to higher Operating Thetan, or OT, levels on a chart called the Bridge to Total Freedom. The highest level released, OT VIII [“eight”], has been taught only aboard a ship called the _Freewinds_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by the science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: This religion’s symbol is a letter S drawn over two triangles. One triangle stands for affinity, reality, and communication, which adherents believe together make up understanding, and the other stands for knowledge, responsibility, and control.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose members believe each person is an immortal spiritual being called a thetan.

tossups.p: This religion teaches that life is driven by eight “dynamics,” or urges toward survival, ranging from the urge to survive as oneself to the urge toward infinity, or a Supreme Being. The eight points of its cross stand for those eight dynamics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard, whose members take part in counseling called auditing.

tossups.p: From 1959 until the mid-1960s, this movement’s founder lived and taught at Saint Hill Manor, a country house in East Grinstead [“GRIN-sted”], England. This movement’s spiritual headquarters, the Flag Land Base, is in Clearwater, Florida.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religious movement founded by L. Ron Hubbard, the author of _Dianetics_.

tossups.p: In 1967, this movement’s founder created a religious order called the Sea Organization and spent several years leading it from ships at sea, including a flagship called the _Apollo_. Members of that order work full-time for this movement’s churches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard, whose followers believe in immortal spiritual beings called thetans.

tossups.p: After this religion’s founder died in 1986, David Miscavige [“mih-SKAV-ij”] became its leader, with the title of chairman of the board of its Religious Technology Center. In 1993, the U.S. Internal Revenue Service recognized its churches as tax-exempt religious organizations.
tossups.r: Its members seek spiritual growth through auditing. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard in the 1950s.

tossups.p: This religion runs a Celebrity Centre in Los Angeles for artists and entertainers. In 2000, one of its best-known members starred in a film based on _Battlefield Earth_, a 1982 science fiction novel by this religion’s founder.
tossups.r: Actors Tom Cruise and John Travolta have been among its best-known members. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: In 1969, this religion helped found the Citizens Commission on Human Rights together with the psychiatrist Thomas Szasz [“SAHS”], reflecting its strong opposition to psychiatry and psychiatric drugs. That group later opened a museum in Los Angeles that criticizes psychiatry.
tossups.r: Its members take part in counseling called auditing. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: This movement’s name combines a Latin word meaning “knowing” with a Greek word meaning “study,” and its founder defined it as “knowing how to know.” He also described it as an “applied religious philosophy.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard, whose members seek to reach a state called Clear.

tossups.p: This religion’s Volunteer Ministers, known for their bright yellow shirts, offer help at disaster sites. Its founder also wrote _The Way to Happiness_, a 1981 booklet of twenty-one moral rules intended for people of any faith.
tossups.r: That founder also wrote _Dianetics_. For 10 points, name this religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard.

tossups.p: This religion’s founder, who was born in Tilden, Nebraska, in 1911, wrote many westerns, adventure tales, and science fiction stories for pulp magazines before he turned to spiritual subjects. Adherents celebrate his birthday every March 13.
tossups.r: That founder was L. Ron Hubbard, the author of _Dianetics_. For 10 points, name this religion he founded.

clues.t: Founded by the American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard (1911–1986)
Grew out of Hubbard’s 1950 bestseller _Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health_
Actors Tom Cruise and John Travolta have been among its best-known members
Its first church opened in Los Angeles in 1954
Adherents believe each person is a thetan, an immortal spiritual being that has lived many past lives
Auditing: one-on-one spiritual counseling with an auditor, who often uses a device called an E-meter
Clear: the state of a person believed to be free of the reactive mind
Hubbard taught that painful experiences leave mental image pictures called engrams in the reactive mind
Spiritual headquarters: the Flag Land Base in Clearwater, Florida
The U.S. Internal Revenue Service recognized its churches as tax-exempt religious organizations in 1993
Dianetics was introduced in _Astounding Science Fiction_ (May 1950), edited by John W. Campbell
Operating Thetan (OT) levels lie beyond Clear on the Bridge to Total Freedom; OT VIII has been taught only aboard the ship _Freewinds_
Symbol: an S over two triangles, for affinity, reality, and communication, and for knowledge, responsibility, and control
Eight dynamics (urges toward survival) range from the self to infinity; the eight points of its cross stand for them
Hubbard lived and taught at Saint Hill Manor in East Grinstead, England, from 1959
The Sea Organization (1967) is its religious order; Hubbard led it from ships such as the _Apollo_
David Miscavige became its leader after Hubbard’s death in 1986
Runs a Celebrity Centre in Los Angeles; a 2000 film of Hubbard’s novel _Battlefield Earth_ starred John Travolta
Opposes psychiatry; helped found the Citizens Commission on Human Rights (1969) with psychiatrist Thomas Szasz
Its name joins Latin for “knowing” and Greek for “study”; Hubbard called it “knowing how to know” and an “applied religious philosophy”
Hubbard’s _The Way to Happiness_ (1981) lists 21 moral rules; its Volunteer Ministers wear yellow shirts at disaster sites
Hubbard was born in Tilden, Nebraska, on March 13, 1911, and wrote pulp westerns and science fiction

trap.title: Not Christian Science
trap.body: Scientology and Christian Science are completely different religions that both have “science” in their names. Christian Science was founded by Mary Baker Eddy in Boston in 1879, publishes the _Christian Science Monitor_, and teaches healing through prayer; Scientology was founded by L. Ron Hubbard in the 1950s. _Dianetics_, Hubbard’s 1950 book and method, came first and is still part of Scientology, so naming it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Thetans, auditing, the E-meter, engrams, Clear, Operating Thetan levels, the Sea Organization, or Clearwater, Florida, mean Scientology. Mary Baker Eddy, the book _Science and Health_, or the _Christian Science Monitor_ means Christian Science.
trap.line: Real answer line: Scientology (or Church of Scientology; prompt on Dianetics; do not accept “Christian Science”)
